title: The attentional blink
hookLine: after three months of practice, meditators missed fewer quick-following signals (Slagter et al.)

cards: Letters flash in the middle of a screen, one after another, very fast. Hidden among them are two numbers, and the task is to report both. The first number appears, and you catch it.
The second comes a split second later, and often it simply isn't there for you. The eyes saw it. The mind didn't.
It's as if attention blinked while still busy with the first. Psychologists gave it exactly that name: the attentional blink.

teach.b: The blink shows that attention is limited not only in space, one thing at a time, but also in time.
Catching something seems to take a moment of processing, and while the mind holds on to the first catch, the next can slip by. Some researchers had treated it as a fixed limit of how minds work.
Then Heleen Slagter and her colleagues, including Richard Davidson, tested people before and after a three-month meditation retreat in the Vipassana style, a practice of watching whatever arises.
A comparison group did the same tests without the retreat. After the retreat, the meditators blinked less: they caught the second number more often. The brain recordings suggested why.
When the first number appeared, the meditators' brains seemed to spend fewer resources on it, leaving more room for what came next.
Notice how they improved: not by grabbing harder, but by grabbing less. They noticed the first thing and let it go a little sooner.
That fits open monitoring: see what arises, don't cling, stay ready for the next. And it reaches past a lab screen.
A sharp word at breakfast, held on to all morning, can blink out the small signals that follow: a child's quiet face, a friend's text that needed an answer.
Honest limits, as always: one study, a lab task, an intensive retreat. But the shape is worth carrying. Less clinging to the first thing.

how: Researchers measure the attentional blink by flashing a rapid stream of letters with two hidden targets and checking how often the second is missed; in Vipassana-style practice, meditators train noticing whatever arises and letting it pass.

practice: Let the breath sit in the background and open your attention to the small things that come and go: a click in the wall, a shift in the light, a twinge in the shoulder.
Note each one and let it go quickly, so you're ready for the next, and see how much you catch when you aren't still holding the last.
